source_text: Exspectabimus nunc ut et amphitheatri repudium de scripturis petamus? si saeuitiam, si impietatem, si feritatem permissam nobis contendere possumus, eamus in amphitheatrum. si tales sumus quales dicimur, delectemur sanguine humano. bonum est cum puniuntur nocentes. quis hoc nisi tamen nocens negabit? et tamen innocentes de supplicio alterius laetari non oportet, cum magis competat innocenti dolere, quod homo, par eius, tam nocens factus est, ut tam crudeliter impendatur. quis autem mihi sponsor est, nocentes semper uel ad bestias uel ad quodcumque supplicium decerni, ut non innocentiae quoque inferatur aut ultione iniudicantis aut infirmitate defensionis aut instantia quaestionis? quam melius ergo est nescire cum mali puniuntur, ne sciam et cum boni pereunt, si tamen bonum sapiunt. certe quidem gladiatores innocentes in ludum ueneunt, ut publicae uoluptatis hostiae fiant. etiam # qui damnantur in ludum, quale est ut de leuiore delicto in homicidas emendatione proficiant? sed haec ethnicis respondi. ceterum absit ut de istius spectaculi auersione diutius discat Christianus. quamquam nemo haec omnia plenius exprimere potest nisi qui adhuc spectat. malo non implere quam meminisse.
thought_title: The amphitheater cannot be defended even by punishment of the guilty
orientation: Tertullian is addressing Christians about the amphitheater, continuing his argument that the shows are incompatible with Christian discipline.
pass_a_gloss: Shall we now wait so that we may also seek a repudiation of the amphitheater from the Scriptures? If we are able to contend that savagery, that impiety, that ferocity is permitted to us, let us go into the amphitheater. If we are such as we are said to be, let us delight in human blood. It is good when the guilty are punished. Who but a guilty man will deny this? And yet it is not fitting for the innocent to rejoice over the punishment of another, since it is more fitting for the innocent to grieve, that a man, his equal, has become so guilty, that he is expended so cruelly. But who is my guarantor, that the guilty are always condemned either to the beasts or to whatever punishment, so that it is not also inflicted upon innocence, either by the vengeance of one judging unjustly, or by the weakness of the defense, or by the urgency of the examination? How much better therefore it is not to know when the wicked are punished, lest I know also when the good perish, if indeed they have a taste for good. Certainly indeed innocent gladiators come into the training school, so that they may become victims of public pleasure. Even those who are condemned to the training school, what sort of thing is it that from a lighter offense they advance into murderers by way of correction? But I have answered these things to the pagans. For the rest, far be it that a Christian should learn any longer about the aversion of this show. Although no one is able to express all these things more fully than he who still watches. I prefer not to fill up than to remember.

choices.why: The word means a formal rejection or divorce; 'repudiation' preserves the legal and formal force of the term.
The verb means to be spent or paid out, suggesting the man's life is spent as a cost; 'is expended' keeps the sense of being used up.
In the context of gladiators, 'ludus' refers to the gladiatorial training school; 'training school' makes this clear.
The word means sacrificial victims; 'victims' preserves the sacrificial connotation of being offered for public pleasure.
The word means turning away from; 'aversion' captures both the act of turning away and the attitude of dislike.

pass_b_english: Should we now wait to seek from the Scriptures a repudiation of the amphitheater as well? If we can claim that savagery, impiety, and ferocity are permitted to us, let us go into the amphitheater. If we are what we are said to be, let us delight in human blood. It is good when the guilty are punished. Who but a guilty man will deny this? And yet even the innocent ought not to rejoice in another's punishment; rather, it befits the innocent to grieve that a man, his equal, has become so guilty that he is expended so cruelly. But who is my guarantor that the guilty are always condemned to the beasts or to whatever punishment, so that it is not also inflicted on innocence, whether through the vengeance of an unjust judge, the weakness of a defense, or the pressure of torture? How much better, then, not to know when the wicked are punished, lest I also know when the good perish—if the good are indeed wise. Certainly, innocent gladiators enter the games to become victims of public pleasure. Even those who are condemned to the games—what sort of correction is it that they advance from a lighter offense into murderers? But I have answered these points to the pagans. For the rest, far be it that a Christian should need longer instruction in turning away from this show. Although no one can express all these things more fully than one who still watches. I prefer not to fill my mind than to remember.
